I built mdkit, a menu bar app for storing and sharing skill markdown files.

Just drop your .md files into mdkit to store them in the cloud, then drag them out whenever you need them.

Share files by email with viewer or editor permissions. Every save is versioned.

Why I built it: I wanted a simple, AI-platform-independent way to share and manage AI skills across teams, with features like editing permissions and version history.

mdkit is in beta and free to try on Windows and Mac.

Genuinely just trying to find out if this is useful for anyone. Would love feedback!

story_text.value:
I used to use Fabricate a long time ago, its strace based build was a great idea and I always wanted something that could track dependencies so I didn't have to.

KIZZ is that, it tracks your dependencies, and also the order of the build. It won't rebuild if nothing changes, and can be scripted with literal markdown files with starlark build steps. I call this building in positive space, not negative space.

Linux only because Win/Mac make doing this very very hard on those platforms. It can also be used to work out dependencies for another build tool, so you're not guessing anymore.

story_text.value:
I made a daily game where you try to identify five Wikipedia articles by looking at their infoboxes with the name and picture hidden. You get one guess per article, and afterwards you get a summary and a link to Wikipedia so at least you might learn something even if you get it wrong!

Infoboxing was inspired by the Wikipedia guessing game Catfishing, which my friends and I love. We play as a group, which is probably cheating, but still sometimes only get like 3/10 correct. Part of the fun is discovering each person's niche and comparing our answers to the rest of the Catfishing audience on the stats page.

I've always wanted to make a daily game and I felt there was still room to explore in the Wikipedia guessing space. In my first prototype I picked out four or five rows from each infobox and revealed them one at a time, but making someone guess repeatedly at something they may never have heard of felt slow, especially across five articles. I ended up following Catfishing's approach: show all the clues with one guess or a skip.

My fiancée and I choose the articles. We started out listing everything we could think of, then explored Wikipedia lists like the "Unusual articles" page and also used AI to suggest candidates in areas we'd missed. In my opinion the best articles have an "a-ha!" moment where it suddenly clicks.

The hardest parts to get right are article curation, balancing the difficulty and deciding what counts as a correct answer. Should "Big Jesus" be an accepted answer for Christ the Redeemer? My fiancée thinks so! I've also put in some rules to try and keep a given day from being too difficult but ultimately it's based on vibes because my idea of what "everyone knows" is biased by my age, gender, region, etc.

The infoboxes are captured ahead of time so I set up a daily check to warn me if an article changes, mainly to catch things like ages changing or people dying. My favourite facepalm moment was when it warned me that Spock had died. His date of death on Wikidata? 2263.

Anyway, give it a go and see what you think. If you have an answer you think should count, tell me through the contact page so that we can keep spoilers out of the comments.

title.value: Show HN: Infoboxing – Guess the Wikipedia article from its infobox

story_text.value:
I built a flashcards app and plugin for obsidian, based on markdown syntax. You use headers and paragraphs, tables or highlighted text to create flashcards and cloze deletions, which you can then review using FSRS algorithm. Everything stays local, it uses a SQL lite db internally to keep track of state and keep the markdown document clean.

I started this project about a year ago when I was facing the problem that I needed flashcards to memorise thousands concepts and language vocabulary I kept forgetting and I hated every flashcards app out there so I decided to build something of my own and I started with markdown and obsidian. Fast forward one year later, I released the iOS and android apps too and a directory for ready made decks to share with people what Im learning, and also help other learners on their journey.

For me it was very interesting to build it because I had to come up with different conventions for what consists a flashcard while limiting myself only to markdown, so that the source text and the flashcard are one thing and they can be read also as a document, without custom syntax or delimiters cluttering it. Im still introducing new features as I explore new possibilities.

I built the foundations myself, algorithms, scheduler, parser. The part that was rough was finding a way to link headers to a state. At first Id just use the hash of the heading text to link it to the state in the database but that would break if you changed the text. So then I tried to use a string similarity algorithm to tie headings to same state, but that caused conflicts. In the end I ended up injecting a static ID on the heading body as a markdown comment. Obsidian hides it in live and reading views and it remains visible only in source mode view. Hate it from a purist perspective but it was a necessary compromise to guarantee a steady state that survives edits.

The app is free on android and as a plugin if you would like to try it. I charge a one time fee of 19.99 on iOS as a way to support the project, in a similar fashion to the Anki model.

Github: https://github.com/dscherdi/decks

I also occasionally post new decks in the directory for anymore interested in flashcards from different topics.

Directory: https://decksmd.app/decks/

Happy to answer any questions you might have.

Thanks for reading!

story_text.value:
Here's why I started building Sikemux:

At first I was using Cursor. The problem with it was, I had to open a new window for each project. That's when Zed came along. It was good and fast. But I didn't like its project switching much, it took me like 2 clicks instead of 1.

I had tried Cursor's agent-first feature as well, but didn't like it much, as I had to see files as well and do git ops with a good layout.

I had even tried tmux + sesh setups then.

That's when I started building Sikemux in Tauri. And project multiplexing got fast and solved, and I was able to see files and do git ops with a good layout of all.

Then came along the Codex App, its browser use and computer use was just tooo damn good, it got hard to go out of that app and try something else. And believe me when I say, I have tried all the ADEs out there. I had then forgot about Sikemux. But after using it for a while, I felt Codex App to be slow at times. It just screamed Electron to me, don't know though whether it's in Tauri or Electron.

I had to revive Sikemux. I then built all of it, great browser use! Fast project multiplexing, seeing files, doing git ops, connectors, agent orchestrator(chief), GUI, GPUI migration, macOS notch, remote hosts, working mobile app with iroh relay to stream everywhere, all in one beautiful window.

title.value: Show HN: Sikemux – a whole team of AI coders in one window (Rust, MIT)

story_text.value:
This is a web app that I built to introduce chess to my children, along with scratching a personal game analysis itch. I link to the games (free, ad free, tracker free, affiliate free, etc), though there is a full learning section as well that was my primary focus. I imagine many here already know the basics of chess.

Of course I leveraged AI in all parts of this project -- and indeed the analysis section uses three separate neural networks to analyze play -- but never without full engagement and co-working between myself and the machine (I've been doing web apps for 30+ years), and all designs are my own. I contrived several of the games wholesale, though others are well trodden in the chess world.

I use chess as a meditative beat from other engagements in my day to day, and have made it a personal mission to break out of the mediocre mid-tier play I've been stuck at for a few years. This has legitimately helped.

I hope this provides some enrichment for others.

story_text.value:
I was new to developing apps with a coding agent months ago. I was sitting in the terminal and trying to understand how people actually use them. I had a bunch of project ideas and was constantly saying, "Do this, do that." For a while it was ok, but later I didn't have enough time to track what my agent was doing.

To find a tracker was not a problem, but to start the agent in a predictable way: in the order of tasks' block links, one at a time per worktree and task, waiting out usage limits, handing a long session over to a fresh one, and keeping going while I'm away questioning me in web chat when it becomes unclear - other solutions couldn't offer me all of it. So that's all Even Keel is doing now - an open-source service on my machine with one web page, under MIT.

It's building itself right now, and my setup starts about 2000 sessions a month. Its own badge in the README shows the numbers, so you can easily check.

Yesterday, it got a huge update and Even Keel can work completely without an external tracker because it has a built-in one. Git is optional. What is required for the first run: Node 24+, one of the agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Copilot CLI), and your imagination.

One time on Windows, Linux or macOS and it installs as a service:

npx even-keel

In Windows PowerShell:

npx.cmd even-keel

The rest of the configuration is on the page.

title.value: Show HN: Even Keel – a task queue for coding agents

story_text.value:
Hi people,

I'm happy to showcase Skif. Skif is a tool for linting JS/TS dependencies, workspace configurations and dead code. Its written in Rust and it started out as a maintained fork of Sherif (a dependency linter which is not actively maintained). In a nutshell it allows the following:

1. Lint and enforce workspace rules for NPM/PNPM/Yarn/Bun workspaces (regular repositories and monorepos). 2. Identify unused dependencies. 3. Enforce dependency policies. 4. Identify dead and unused code.

It is substantially faster than the 3 above mentioned tools, and it was hardened on several very large repositories to ensure it has better precision.

You can read more in the readme and the docs.

Happy to answer questions!

title.value: Show HN: Skif – An ultra fast alternative to Knip, Sherif and Syncpack

story_text.value:
Rally is a multi-player platform to build reactive micro-applications together that connects event streams to agents that then update the artifact. We've had pilots build a PR dashboard that sorts by risk assessment (an agent actually reads the code) per PR, a micro-CRM that pulls in live deals from multiple Gmail inboxes, and a shared grocery list that groups items by store aisle.

We're similar to Muse's Spaces, Google's TableTop, and the standard artifacts most harnesses now support. Our differentiator is being multi-player so groups can iterate together, artifacts calling agents on incoming events so updates can be more sophisticated than an API call, and giving artifacts a full application stack.

Under the hood, each artifact is a Cloudflare Durable Object with its own SQLite database, compute, and storage.

As an example this is our podcast artifact that helps us keep up-to-date on what happened on the repo each day https://connected-tidy-crystalline-haldane-g.rallyuserconten...

GitHub: https://github.com/juno-ai-labs/avalon
